# Umbraco Rules

Project conventions, enforced by code in `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco` where possible. The short version of the ten UmbraCommandments.

1. **Never put content behind a composition.** Removing a composition permanently deletes its content on every document that used it — no recovery through revisions. Compositions are for meta, settings, CTAs. Litmus test: *if we remove this composition later, is what remains still viable content?*
2. **There are six kinds of document type — file each in its folder.** Page (renders), Block (renders; lives in block list/grid; never used as a composition), Composition (composed onto others; never rendered, never pickable), Data (element; never renders — settings, events, people), Repository (container node; never renders), Repository Item (the pickable records inside a Repository).
3. **Data types never sit at the root of the data type tree.** Built-ins under `/Umbraco/<editor>`, custom ones under `/Custom/<editor>`. `DataTypeSavedHandler` enforces this on every save.
4. **Register in an `IComposer`, not Program.cs.** If `IUmbracoBuilder` can do it, it belongs in `Composers/`. Non-Umbraco concerns (CORS, App Insights) go in `WebApplicationBuilder` extension methods.
5. **Production runs in production mode.** Umbraco Application Url set, `--configuration Release`, HTTPS only, no model generation, no template editing. `appsettings.json` ships configured this way — don't soften it; put dev conveniences in `appsettings.Development.json`.
6. **Aliases are English and camelCase.** No exceptions.
7. **Dictionary keys are PascalCase with dots** (`My.Dictionary.Item`), and a dictionary folder never has values of its own.
8. **Media always lives in a folder.**
9. **The content root only holds Repositories.** The site hangs under the WWW `siteRoot` node; going multi-site means adding another Page beneath it, not re-architecting. Because WWW never renders, the site Page needs a **domain** or nothing answers on `/` — assign `/` for a single site, a hostname each for several.
10. **uSync everything — commit `Umbraco.Bench.Umbraco/uSync/`.** Export is automatic; you should not need to trigger it. On Umbraco Cloud, use Umbraco Deploy instead.

<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net10.0</TargetFramework>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
    <CompressionEnabled>false</CompressionEnabled> <!-- Disable compression. E.g. for umbraco backoffice files. These files should be precompressed by node and not let dotnet handle it -->
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageReference Include="Umbraco.Cms" />
    <PackageReference Include="uSync" />
  </ItemGroup>

  <PropertyGroup>
    <!--
      Opt-in to app-local ICU to ensure consistent globalization APIs across different platforms.
      Default mirrors prior behaviour introduced in https://github.com/umbraco/Umbraco-CMS/pull/11276: enabled unless building on macOS without an explicit RuntimeIdentifier.
      To override:
        * Build/publish:  dotnet publish -p:UmbracoUseAppLocalIcu=false
        * Post-publish:   edit System.Globalization.AppLocalIcu in the published *.runtimeconfig.json
      Note: DOTNET_SYSTEM_GLOBALIZATION_APPLOCALICU is only honored when AppLocalIcu is absent from runtimeconfig.json
      (verified on .NET 10) — the general .NET 9 env-var-precedence rule does not apply to this knob, since it is
      resolved by the native host before the CLR boots. Use one of the two override paths above instead.
      Keep UmbracoAppLocalIcuVersion in sync with the referenced Microsoft.ICU.ICU4C.Runtime package version.
    -->
    <UmbracoUseAppLocalIcu Condition="'$(UmbracoUseAppLocalIcu)' == '' and ($(RuntimeIdentifier.StartsWith('linux')) or $(RuntimeIdentifier.StartsWith('win')) or ('$(RuntimeIdentifier)' == '' and !$([MSBuild]::IsOSPlatform('osx'))))">true</UmbracoUseAppLocalIcu>
    <UmbracoUseAppLocalIcu Condition="'$(UmbracoUseAppLocalIcu)' == ''">false</UmbracoUseAppLocalIcu>
    <UmbracoAppLocalIcuVersion Condition="'$(UmbracoAppLocalIcuVersion)' == ''">72.1.0.3</UmbracoAppLocalIcuVersion>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup Condition="'$(UmbracoUseAppLocalIcu)' == 'true'">
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.ICU.ICU4C.Runtime" />
    <RuntimeHostConfigurationOption Include="System.Globalization.AppLocalIcu" Value="$(UmbracoAppLocalIcuVersion)" />
  </ItemGroup>


  <PropertyGroup>
    <!-- Razor files are needed for the backoffice to work correctly -->
    <CopyRazorGenerateFilesToPublishDirectory>true</CopyRazorGenerateFilesToPublishDirectory>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <!-- Keep the local appsettings.json override out of publish output -->
    <Content Update="appsettings.Local.json" CopyToPublishDirectory="Never" />
  </ItemGroup>


</Project>

properties.heading: Why MCP is Awesome: Part 1
properties.subheading: The Model Context Protocol revolutionizes AI integration

content.markup:
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a game-changer for AI applications. It provides a standardized way for AI models to interact with external tools, APIs, and data sources, creating a seamless integration experience.

In this first part of our series, we explore how MCP bridges the gap between AI and the real world. By defining a simple protocol, MCP allows AI assistants to read from and write to external systems without needing custom integrations for each service.

Key Benefits of MCP:

  • Standardization: One protocol to rule them all - no more custom integrations
  • Flexibility: Works with any tool or API that implements the protocol
  • Security: Built-in authentication and permission systems
  • Extensibility: Easy to add new tools and capabilities

With MCP, AI applications can finally break free from their isolated environments and interact with the world around them in a structured, secure way.

properties.heading: Why MCP is Awesome: Part 2
properties.subheading: Building the future of AI integration

content.markup:
In Part 1, we introduced the Model Context Protocol and its benefits. Now, let's dive deeper into how MCP is transforming the AI landscape.

MCP isn't just about connecting AI to tools - it's about creating an ecosystem where AI can truly understand and interact with context. By providing structured access to external resources, MCP enables AI to make better decisions, provide more accurate information, and perform more complex tasks.

Real-World Applications:

  • Content Management: AI can read and write to CMS systems like Umbraco
  • Data Analysis: Access databases and spreadsheets for insights
  • API Integration: Connect to any REST or GraphQL API
  • File Management: Read and write files with proper permissions

The beauty of MCP is its simplicity. Developers don't need to learn complex frameworks or write custom connectors. They simply implement the MCP protocol, and their tools become instantly accessible to any AI that supports it.

As we look to the future, MCP has the potential to become the standard for AI integration, much like HTTP became the standard for web communication. The possibilities are endless, and we're just getting started.
